e.t: Aalaph or Aalaf is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs once in this Greek Old Testament corpus, at Judges 1:31. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its particular contextual significance cannot be stated beyond identifying the name in that passage.

Addara, also rendered Aththara, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its more precise role in that passage cannot be described; its established lexical sense is simply the name Addara or Aththara.

Akkos is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than describing a general quality or action. The name is rendered as “Akkōs” or “Akkos,” preserving it as a personal designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:17. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person’s particular role, but the word itself functions simply as a name.

Aleph is the name of a Hebrew letter, used here as a noun rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalm 118:1. The supplied lexical meaning identifies it simply as “aleph”; without the verse text, no further contextual significance should be assigned to this occurrence. Its role is therefore best understood as identifying the letter-name itself within the Psalm’s structure.

This noun refers to aloes, a fragrant plant or aromatic substance known in the biblical world. Its meaning is straightforward: it names the material itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Song of Songs 4:14. Because the available information does not include the verse text or its surrounding passage, the word’s precise poetic role there cannot be described here. Its central sense remains “aloes,” an aromatic botanical substance mentioned among valued fragrances.

Amessias is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 16 times across 15 verses, all in 2 Kings. The available lexical information gives the name itself—“Amessias”—without an additional definition or description. Its precise identity and role in any particular passage must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and account.

This Greek LXX noun means “refreshing,” describing relief or renewed ease. It names the experience of being refreshed rather than an action performed by someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 8:11. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there, but the word itself points to restoration from weariness, distress, or discomfort. Its basic sense is therefore a welcome renewal or relief, expressed as something received or experienced.

This Greek LXX verb means “blossom” or “bloom”—to produce flowers or fresh growth. It describes the visible flourishing of plants and can portray something springing into life or reaching a season of beauty. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, including passages in Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Its ordinary sense remains focused on flowering, budding, or flourishing rather than merely existing or growing. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something unnoticed or done without solemnity—that is, without public ceremony or formal observance. It points to a lack of notice or solemn form rather than naming a person, action, or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:36. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is something quiet, unmarked, or lacking solemn recognition.

This verb means “depart”: to leave or go away from a place or person. It describes movement away rather than arrival or remaining. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times—three times in Genesis and once in Hosea—so its basic sense is consistent across these passages. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself straightforwardly expresses departure.

This Greek verb means to “carry away” or “escort”—to take someone or something from one place to another, either by removal or by accompanying them. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This verb means to scare away—to drive someone or something off through fear or intimidation. It describes an action that causes another person, animal, or group to leave rather than remain. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including passages from Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the action is directed against.

This verb means “whistle aloud.” It names an action—what someone does—rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:14. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the act of whistling aloud. No broader meaning should be attached to it without contextual support.

“Architect” means a person identified by that professional role—the word is a noun for an architect. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, showing that it names a recognized kind of skilled worker rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

Asidōn, also rendered Asithon, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a particular person or name-bearing individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:29. Without the verse text and its surrounding context, the name itself does not provide further information about the individual’s role or significance.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Atad” and also identified as “Atath.” It functions as a name rather than a general descriptive term. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 50:10–11. The available record identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about what it names.

This Greek LXX noun means “locust,” referring to the familiar insect. It names the creature itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Nahum 3:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: a locust. Scripture’s use of this term is therefore specific and concrete, identifying a particular kind of insect.

Barea or Varea is a proper name—the name of a particular person or place—rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs three times: once in Esther, once in Sirach, and once in 3 Maccabees. The lexical meaning identifies the name as “Barea” or “Varea,” while the surrounding verse context is needed to determine exactly whom or what it identifies in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “blaspheme; defame”: to speak against someone in a dishonoring or abusive way. It can describe words that attack a person’s name, reputation, or honor, including speech directed against God. As a verb, it expresses the act of making such a charge or insult rather than merely holding a negative opinion. It occurs seven times in this LXX corpus, across five Old Testament and two deuterocanonical verses.

This word is a proper name rendered “Bouzites” or “Vuzitis.” It functions as a name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job 32, appearing in Job 32:2 and Job 32:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference cannot be explained further, but its basic role is to identify the named figure or designation represented by this proper name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaian” or “Yean.” It identifies a named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:28. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine whether the referent is a person, place, or another named entity; that must be established from the surrounding passage. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context in which the name appears.

This noun refers to the creator—the one who brings existence into being. It can be expressed as “creator” or “author of existence,” emphasizing the source and origin of what exists rather than merely describing someone who makes an ordinary object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Wisdom 13:5. Its precise force in that passage is understood from the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a designation for the one responsible for existence itself.

This adverb means “legitimately.” It describes an action, statement, or claim as being done or presented in a legitimate manner. Its role is to tell the reader how something occurs, not to name a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Both occurrences are in the deuterocanonical section of this corpus.

This noun means “corner,” referring to the point or angular part where two sides meet. It can describe a physical corner in a structure or another defined edge or extremity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 31 times across 30 verses, so its basic sense is used in descriptions of buildings, furnishings, cities, and other things with corners. The exact reference of the corner depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself consistently points to a corner or angular boundary.

This Greek LXX verb means “stoop and creep through.” It describes moving forward while bent low, apparently because the passage or movement requires someone to lower himself and proceed in a confined or difficult way. The word occurs 10 times across 9 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, so it expresses a specific physical action rather than a broad abstract idea. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or thing being described.

This Greek LXX adjective means “speaking two languages.” It describes someone able to use two languages, rather than naming an action, place, or object. In this corpus, it occurs five times: once in Proverbs and four times in Sirach. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains focused on a person’s ability to speak two languages.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ebraia” or “Evrea.” It functions as a personal name or designation rather than as a general description. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times: twice in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy. The available information identifies the name and its use as a proper noun, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the particular person or situation in each occurrence.

This word means “fortitude”: steady strength and courage that enable a person to remain firm under pressure. As a noun, it names this quality of resolute endurance rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:34. The reference identifies its single occurrence, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the word functions in that specific passage.

This noun refers to being away from one's homeland or living in exile. It describes a person's condition of being abroad, separated from the place where they normally belong. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 4:11. That reference identifies where it appears, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific force there. Its central meaning remains the state of being abroad or in exile.

This Greek LXX verb means “boil over”: to become intensely heated and rise or overflow, like something boiling. It describes an action or process rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, across passages from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something boiling up beyond its normal bounds.

“Burn out” describes something being consumed or exhausted by fire, or the action of burning until it is spent. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 52 times across 50 verses. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is burning and how the surrounding sentence presents the action.

This word means “voluntarily”: doing something by personal choice and willingness rather than by compulsion. As an adverb, it describes how an action is carried out, emphasizing that the person acts freely or of their own accord. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Exodus, Psalms, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the action and surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains willing, self-directed action.

Ellis is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in the list of David’s mighty men at 2 Samuel 23:26. The name itself identifies that individual; its precise significance beyond identifying him is not given here. It should therefore be understood as a personal designation, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

This word means “me,” referring to the speaker as the person affected by, involved in, or receiving an action. It is a pronoun, so it stands in place of the speaker’s name or identity within a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 236 times, showing that it is a common way for someone to refer to himself or herself. Its exact role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains the speaker as the object or person being addressed in the sentence.

This verb means “give in,” expressing the act of yielding when resistance or opposition comes to an end. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action rather than a person or thing: someone or something gives way. It occurs four times across three verses in the LXX. Its precise force depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains yielding rather than automatically implying approval, weakness, or agreement.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “take a pledge from”—to receive something as security for a debt or obligation. It describes the act of requiring or accepting pledged property, rather than simply taking something for no stated reason. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, across seven verses, especially in laws and passages addressing treatment of the poor, debtors, or vulnerable people. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains receiving a pledge as security.

This verb means “value in”: it expresses treating someone or something as worthy of regard, honor, or esteem. As a verb, it describes the action of assigning worth rather than merely recognizing that worth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Kings 1:13–14. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is valuing or honoring someone.

This Greek LXX noun means “dream”: an experience or vision received while sleeping. It names dreams in a straightforward way, whether they are simply reported or connected with a message that requires interpretation. The word occurs 77 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it describes a recurring biblical subject rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This Greek LXX verb means “burst out insolently”: it describes an abrupt expression or action marked by insolence rather than respectful restraint. The word presents insolence as something that breaks out openly and forcefully. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, across two Old Testament passages and one deuterocanonical passage, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “cast at” or “throw upon.” It describes the action of directing or placing something onto another person or thing. As a verb, it focuses on the act itself rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:26; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what was cast or thrown and how the action functions there.

The word is an adjective meaning “sevenfold.” It describes something in terms of seven, such as a sevenfold measure or character. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel 12:6 and Psalm 78:12. Its precise role is determined by the sentence, but its central idea remains something expressed as sevenfold. It qualifies whatever person, thing, or action the surrounding context places alongside it.

The Greek LXX verb means “empty itself; vomit.” It describes expelling contents rather than merely being full or present. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 7:28; the word’s precise force there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the word alone. Its basic sense remains the act of emptying itself or vomiting.

This verb describes someone or something as being of good repute—that is, regarded favorably or considered worthy of approval. It expresses a positive standing rather than merely an outward appearance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times: once in Genesis and three times in Sirach. Its normal sense remains “of good repute,” while the surrounding verse determines exactly what or who is being described. The word appears in Genesis 43:23, Sirach 39:34, Sirach 40:25, and Sirach 41:16.

This adjective means “well-aimed,” describing something directed accurately toward its intended target. It portrays purposeful direction rather than random or wandering movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:21; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what is being described there. Its basic meaning remains focused and accurately directed, whether referring to an object, action, or force.

Zaraia, also rendered Zarea, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies an individual. The name occurs five times across four verses in the Septuagint, appearing in 1 Chronicles and Ezra. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it does not establish which person is meant in each occurrence or add a separate meaning beyond this personal designation.

This Greek LXX verb expresses being “here”—a presence at a stated place or point in the narrative. It is used 226 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, so it is a recurring way to indicate that someone or something is present at a location. The surrounding verse determines who is present and why that presence matters.

Thanthanai is a proper name, referring to a person named Thanthanai, also rendered Thanthane. It is not presented as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is to identify an individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Ezra: Ezra 5:3, Ezra 5:6, and Ezra 6:13. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual role should be assigned to the name.

Thelmeleth is a proper name used to identify a specific named entity. Its meaning is preserved as the name “Thelmeleth,” rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Ezra 2:59 and once in Nehemiah 7:61. The available wording does not identify whether Thelmeleth names a person, family, place, or another entity, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “hold religious observances” or “observe religiously.” It describes carrying out acts of worship or religious practice, focusing on the observance itself rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in the Wisdom of Solomon. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the deliberate practice of religious observance.

Iasa is a proper name appearing in the Greek Old Testament. The name identifies someone or something called Iasa, but the name alone does not tell us whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. It occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Judges 11:20 and once in 1 Chronicles 6:63. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is the proper name “Iezraēl” or “Iezrel,” referring to a person or place named Jezreel rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the word’s specific referent in that passage cannot be identified further from the name alone. Its basic function is simply to designate Jezreel within that one recorded occurrence.

This noun refers to a group of people gathered together—a “crowd” or “band.” It describes people viewed collectively rather than as separate individuals. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in 2 Maccabees 5:3. Its basic meaning remains broad enough to describe an assembled group without specifying why they gathered, how large they were, or whether their purpose was peaceful or hostile.

This adjective means “doing bad,” describing a person or action characterized by wrongdoing. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Proverbs, so its recorded use is limited but consistent. It identifies what is morally wrong rather than naming a particular kind of wrongdoing. The surrounding wording determines whether it describes a person, conduct, or deeds in a given verse.

This Greek LXX noun means “nut tree,” referring to a tree that bears nuts. It names the tree itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing once each in Genesis, Numbers, and Song of Songs. Its specific sense in any particular verse is best understood from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a nut-bearing tree.

gl: that which is to be devoured; food
d: that which is to be devoured; food

e.t: This Greek Old Testament noun means “that which is to be devoured; food.” It refers to something intended to be eaten or consumed, functioning as a name for the food itself rather than an action. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, with most occurrences in Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something available for eating or devouring.

This Greek verb means “leave off; end.” It describes bringing an action, activity, or period to a close, with attention to stopping rather than beginning. As a verb, it expresses what someone or something does when it ceases or reaches its conclusion. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees 9:5 and 3 Maccabees 6:32. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “flow down”: it describes something moving downward in a stream or descending course. The word focuses on the direction and movement of what comes down, rather than simply being below. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is described as moving downward.

This adjective describes someone or something as “dominant”—having commanding strength, power, or authority. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings to portray a force or presence that prevails rather than one that is weak or easily overcome. The word occurs 61 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, so its central idea appears across many passages while retaining this basic sense of powerful superiority. The exact nuance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “steering”: the act of directing or guiding something toward its proper course. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Proverbs, where the word belongs to the language of wise direction and counsel. Its basic sense is practical guidance—helping determine a course and keep it moving rightly. The surrounding verse supplies the specific application each time.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut.” It describes the action of cutting, without adding a more specific object or method to the basic meaning. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, in 12 verses, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare term. Its exact sense in a particular passage depends on what is being cut and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of cutting. The word is found from Exodus through Isaiah in the Greek Old Testament.

Ransom means a payment or required price given to secure someone’s release or recovery. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun refers to the value set in place when a person, life, or possession is released from a claim or obligation. It occurs 19 times across 18 verses, especially in legal instructions concerning compensation, redemption, and the restoration of property or freedom. The word therefore centers on a price that answers a claim and makes release possible, rather than on release viewed apart from its cost.

Mazar is a proper name, not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name rather than a general concept or instruction. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Genesis 36:42. The name alone does not support a more specific claim about the individual or referent it identifies without the surrounding verse text.

Mainam, also rendered Menam, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 15:24. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough context here to determine whether Mainam refers specifically to a person or a location. Its precise identification therefore belongs to the surrounding passage.

Malōch, also rendered Malokh, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It does not function as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its significance comes from the person identified rather than from a broader dictionary meaning. In this corpus, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:29. Without the verse text and surrounding genealogy, the name alone does not support further claims about that person.

This noun means “greatness,” referring to impressive magnitude, stature, or excellence. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used to speak of greatness associated with God, his works, or what he accomplishes, and it can also describe the notable scale of people or plans. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including its deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense is not a specific emotion or action, but the quality of being great or distinguished; the surrounding verse determines what possesses that greatness.

This noun means “transferal” or “alteration”—a change in where something is placed, how it is arranged, or what form it takes. It describes a movement or modification rather than an object or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:24. The surrounding verse text is not available, so its precise force in that occurrence must be determined from the passage itself; its basic lexical idea remains a transfer or change.

gl: changing one's abode; emigrating and settling elsewhere
d: changing one's abode; emigrating and settling elsewhere

e.t: This noun refers to “changing one's abode; emigrating and settling elsewhere.” It describes relocation from one residence to another, with the idea of establishing oneself in the new place rather than making a temporary visit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 20:3. The exact force of the word there depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains someone who changes residence and settles elsewhere.

Milētos is a proper name, rendered as “Milētos” or “Militos.” It identifies a particular named place or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 27:18. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise reference cannot be described further; its lexical function is simply to name Milētos. This Greek LXX word should be understood as a proper name within the LXX, not merged with similarly rendered words from another corpus.

This noun means “innermost place” or “inmost nook,” referring to the deepest or most secluded part of something. It describes a location rather than an action, emotion, or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom, so its meaning is focused and concrete rather than broad or frequently repeated. The surrounding verse determines what physical or figurative place is being called the innermost part.

Naanan is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. It appears once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 12:24. Because the available information gives the name itself but not the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage. The name should therefore be read as a proper name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

This Greek LXX noun means “conquest”—the gaining of victory over an opponent or the successful overcoming of resistance. It presents victory as an achieved result, especially in settings involving conflict or opposition. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains an accomplished conquest or triumph.

Noua, also rendered Nua, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears five times in the LXX, in Numbers, Joshua, and Judges. Its precise significance in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text, but the lexical meaning supplied here is simply the personal name Noua or Nua.

This LXX Greek noun means “lodging”: a place or provision for someone to stay. It names the accommodation connected with housing a person, rather than describing the person who stays there. In this LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense remains consistent while the surrounding passage determines the particular situation. It appears in books including 2 Samuel, Hosea, Sirach, and Maccabees.

This Greek LXX noun means “act of dwelling; habitation,” referring to living in or occupying a place. It can describe a dwelling itself or the condition of residing there, depending on the sentence. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including Deuteronomy, 2 Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on residence or a dwelling place rather than travel, possession, or a person.

This word means “talons,” the sharp claws of a bird or animal. It is a noun used for a physical feature that grips, tears, or holds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, including passages describing animals and imagery involving birds. Its basic meaning remains concrete: the pointed claws at the end of an animal’s feet. The surrounding passage determines whether the word refers to an actual animal or uses the image in a comparison.

Orthosia is a proper name, referring to “Orthōsia,” also rendered “Orthosia.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify a particular person, place, or other named entity in the text. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:37. The reference identifies where the name appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what named entity it identifies there.

gl: cake of preserved fruit; fruit cake
d: cake of preserved fruit; fruit cake

e.t: This Greek LXX noun means a cake made from preserved fruit—a compact food prepared for eating or giving. It refers to a particular kind of food rather than to a person, action, or abstract idea. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages connected with provisions, gifts, or food brought to someone. Its exact role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a fruit cake or cake of preserved fruit.

This verb means “defer” or “carried away.” It describes an action in which something is put off or moved away, depending on the sentence. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in 1 Samuel and once in Ezra. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, its precise sense in each occurrence cannot be stated more narrowly. Its basic idea remains an action of deferring or being carried away, rather than a noun naming a person, object, or place.

This Greek LXX noun means “sadness,” describing the condition or experience of being sad. It names an emotional response that can be expressed personally or shared by a community. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used across many passages rather than referring to only one particular event. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament verb refers to using a “plate” or “blindfold,” describing something placed over or around another thing. Its basic idea is covering or concealing rather than revealing. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages connected with Exodus and 1 Kings. The exact force depends on what is being covered in each passage, but the central sense remains a covering object or action.

This noun means “breastplate,” referring to a garment worn across the chest. It names an object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Exodus 28:4. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while its particular significance in that passage belongs to the passage’s wider description.

This noun refers to fixing something in place or constructing it. It describes the act of putting something together, establishing it, or making it firm rather than the finished object itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 41:20; the surrounding verse text is needed to determine its precise use there. Its central idea remains the work of fixing or building something into an established form.
